title: We Need a New Purity Culture. Here's What It Should Look Like
author: Samuel D. James
summary: Samuel D. James, writing for First Things and republished via Digital Liturgies, argues that evangelical purity culture deserves rehabilitation rather than the wholesale rejection it has received from both secular and exvangelical critics. He grants the movement's real excesses, particularly its excessive stigmatization of sexual feeling and its shame-driven accountability-group culture, while arguing that its critics forget the historical context: a genuine 1990s crisis of AIDS deaths, record teen pregnancy, and a coarsening public square that purity culture was responding to, however imperfectly. His proposal for a new purity culture pivots the emphasis for a changed cultural moment, since today's more sexually cautious Gen Z and Gen Alpha need to be taught the beauty of marriage rather than warned off promiscuity, and it insists shame be used only protectively, never as a motivational tool. The piece closes by extending purity culture's relevance into the AI era, arguing that emerging "relationships with chatbots" are a symptom of aloneness that Christian community, not condemnation, must address.
points: Argues purity culture's critics conflate its genuine excesses with its underlying biblical convictions, and that the movement was a real, if imperfect, response to a documented 1990s crisis (peak AIDS deaths among young men, record teen pregnancy).

Distinguishes just from unjust shame: 'A new evangelical purity culture must take a new approach to shame, using it as a protective tool when necessary, but never as a motivational tool,' criticizing pornography accountability groups built on public confession.

Argues the cultural moment has flipped: Gen Z and Alpha are less sexually active than their parents' generation, so today's task is teaching the beauty of marriage rather than warning teens off promiscuity.

Extends the purity-culture framework into the AI era, predicting that within five years most evangelical churches will have members in chatbot relationships, framing 'digital philandering' as a symptom of aloneness community must address.
quotes: Evangelical purity culture is tricky to define, but it usually refers to a trend of the 1980s and 1990s that prioritized sexual abstinence and modesty and expressed this emphasis through preaching, parenting, and publishing.
By the early years of 1990s, AIDS had become the number one cause of death for United States men ages 25 to 44, and the teen pregnancy rate had reached an all-time high.
Today's teens don't need to be warned off sex; they need to be taught the beauty of conjugal love. The most effective way to promote purity is by promoting marriage.
A new evangelical purity culture must take a new approach to shame, using it as a protective tool when necessary, but never as a motivational tool.

It is likely that in five years, just about every evangelical church will have at least a few members who are in relationships with chatbots. A Christian purity culture for the AI era must recognize that digital philandering is often a symptom of aloneness.
